prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a layered layout: the table, bowl, spoon, and the camera wearer’s forearms/hands are nearest (roughly 0.2–0.8 m), the laptop and nearby chairs are at about 1–2 m, and the staircase, walls, and distant furniture are several metres behind them. Across frames 1–3, the bowl stays within arm’s reach and shifts from near centre to the right and then lower-centre as the wearer turns; in frames 4–5 the laptop appears on the left at roughly 0.8–1.3 m, while the wearer’s raised hand becomes the closest object and partly occludes it. Brightness makes foreground distance ordering and occlusion boundaries clearer than RGB alone, including the forearms in front of the bowl/table and the hand in front of the laptop. Exact metre estimates are uncertain because the map provides relative monocular depth rather than scale, and several boundaries—especially the spoon, chair edges, and distant dark regions—look smoothed or incomplete.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map separates nearby instances: a person mask corresponding mainly to the camera wearer’s visible arms/body area, one or more bowl masks, a spoon and knife-like utensil, chairs, the dining table, and later a laptop; most background architecture remains unlabeled. It makes left/right overlap explicit: in frames 1–2 the hands/arms flank and partly occlude the bowl, with the utensils above/right of it, while by frame 3 the bowl is lower-right and the table dominates the foreground; in frames 4–5 the laptop is left-of-centre and the raised hand/person mask overlaps it. The bowl and utensils are within the wearer’s reach (about 0.2–0.8 m), the laptop and nearest chairs are roughly 0.8–2 m away, and background chairs are farther apart and several metres away; no other person is clearly segmented as a complete, independently located figure, so facing direction or gaze toward the wearer cannot be established. The map is unreliable where labels flicker or conflict—such as duplicate bowl/chair labels, a knife label where RGB appears spoon-like, a toilet label in frame 5, fragmented masks, and objects cut off at frame edges—so it is stronger for instance separation than for metric distance.
descriptions.pose: The pose map contains almost no full-body evidence: a small magenta hand trace appears near the centre in frame 2, and a much larger magenta hand skeleton with nearby yellow body/keypoint detections appears on the right in frame 5; the other frames are essentially empty. It therefore clarifies articulated hand position where RGB is ambiguous: the frame-2 hand is near the bowl within arm’s reach, while in frame 5 the raised hand is very close to the camera (roughly 0.2–0.5 m), right-of-centre, and in front of/partly occluding the laptop area. The larger shift from the small central detection to the large right-side detection is consistent with the hand moving closer and rightward as the camera wearer turns, but the sparse detections do not support reliable estimates of whole-body orientation, interpersonal distance, or whether anyone faces or looks toward the wearer. Missing skeletons in frames 1, 3, and 4, disconnected yellow points, and the incomplete frame-5 hand make this map unreliable for scene layout or precise motion beyond the detected limbs.
